title: Simon's Secret Saudi Deal: OPEC Surpluses Become a Standing Bid Under US Debt
participants: US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: When the 1973–74 embargo roughly quadrupled oil prices, Saudi Arabia and other OPEC members accumulated large dollar surpluses with no established outlet. The US fiscal apparatus, running deficits and needing buyers for Treasury debt, stood to profit up front from capturing those surpluses as a standing bid under its debt issuance.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Treasury Secretary William E. Simon led the 1974 Saudi negotiations that opened US Treasury purchases to the Saudis, with oil priced in dollars generating the surplus in the first place. The June 1974 US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation institutionalised the financial and military relationship, binding surplus recycling to security guarantees.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The arrangement was secret at the time; it was only reconstructed decades later from released official files and Simon's own memoirs. Because the recycling ran through routine Treasury purchases rather than any announced treaty, the mechanism stayed invisible to the public and regulators — and must be carefully separated from the unsupported 'secret treaty binding oil to the dollar' version.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was structural US fiscal capacity: OPEC surpluses became a standing bid under US debt, locking in the government's ability to finance itself through the decade. The Saudis and OPEC held the recycled assets; the US Treasury held the guaranteed demand for its paper.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The arrangement was laundered through the bland institutional form of the Joint Commission and normalized as ordinary Treasury market operations. Because the strong 'secret treaty' claim is unsupported, public debate fixates on the conspiracy version — while the documented recycling ledger line is never truly accounted for as a policy choice with distributional consequences.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The post-1971 end-of-Bretton-Woods dollar and the prior US-Saudi security relationship formed the inheritance; oil was already priced in dollars when the embargo struck.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A new framework of petrodollar surplus recycling — OPEC surpluses channeled into US Treasuries — institutionalised via the June 1974 US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Dollar payments for oil flowed to OPEC, and the surpluses rolled back into US Treasury debt, financing the deficits of the decade and sustaining the dollar's reserve role — proceeds and positions feeding the next round of issuance.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The standing foreign bid under US debt established the fiscal capacity and secrecy precedent that later dossiers on deficit finance and conduit structures build upon.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The pop-culture version holds that a secret 1974 treaty bound Saudi oil to the dollar by explicit pact, a hidden cabal deal engineered by Simon and the Saudis, often styled as the origin of the 'petrodollar conspiracy.'
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The secret-treaty frame erases the documented mechanism: routine, secret-at-the-time Treasury purchases negotiated by Simon and institutionalised through the Joint Commission. By chasing a nonexistent treaty, the decoy hides the real ledger — surplus recycling through Treasuries that locked in structural US fiscal capacity through the decade.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: In 1974, following the 1973–74 oil embargo that roughly quadrupled prices, Saudi Arabia and other OPEC members held large dollar surpluses with nowhere established to put them. Treasury Secretary William E. Simon led secret Saudi negotiations opening US Treasury purchases to the Saudis — an arrangement reconstructed decades later from released official files and Simon's memoirs. The US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation (June 1974) institutionalised the financial and military relationship. The documented mechanism was surplus recycling through Treasuries with oil priced in dollars; OPEC surpluses became a standing bid under US debt, locking in structural US fiscal capacity through the decade. The strong 'secret treaty binding oil to the dollar' version is unsupported.
